H1.text: A potato sprouting in the kitchen basket. A knob of ginger. A cucumber vine curling around a stick.

H2.text: None of them looks like a stem. No tall green stick, no branches in the air.

H3.text: Diya asked: a potato grows under the soil, just like a root. So why do books call it a stem?

H4.text: Because a stem is not decided by where it grows. It is decided by what it carries: nodes and buds.

H5.text: By the end, you will spot a stem in any disguise: under the soil, as a tendril, a thorn, or a flat green pad.

D1.text: First, where does a stem come from? Inside every seed sits a tiny baby shoot, called the plumule. It grows up into the stem.

D2.text: A stem has nodes: the points where leaves grow. The part of the stem between two nodes is called an internode.

D3.text: A stem also carries buds. A bud at the tip is a terminal bud. A bud in the axil, the angle between a leaf and the stem, is an axillary bud.

D4.text: The stem holds out the branches, leaves, flowers and fruits. It carries water, minerals and food through the plant.

D5.text: Some stems also store food, give support or protection, or make new plants. For those jobs, they change their shape.

Z1.text: Let's test the potato. Zoom in under the soil of a potato plant.

Z2.text: The potatoes grow at the tips of thin underground stems. Each potato is a swollen stem tip, packed with stored food. It is called a tuber.

Z3.text: Now look closely at the skin. Those small dents are the eyes of the potato.

Z4.text: Each eye is a node, with buds sitting in it. A root never has nodes like these.

Z5.text: Leave a potato in the basket, and the buds in its eyes sprout into new shoots. That is a stem at work.

P1.text: Now let's meet stems in disguise, one job at a time.

P2.text: Storing food. Potato, ginger, turmeric, zaminkand and Colocasia are underground stems that store food.

P3.text: They also help the plant survive a bad season, like a dry summer, and grow again later. This is called perennation.

P4.text: Climbing. In gourds like cucumber and pumpkin, and in grapevines, axillary buds grow into stem tendrils: thin, coiled springs that wrap around a support.

P5.text: Protection. In Citrus and Bougainvillea, axillary buds turn into thorns: woody, straight and pointed. They keep grazing animals away.

P6.text: Making food. In dry places, Opuntia has a flat green stem, and Euphorbia a fleshy round one. They have chlorophyll, so they make food by photosynthesis.

P7.text: Spreading. In mint and jasmine, a thin side branch grows for a while, then arches down to touch the ground, and roots there.

P8.text: Pistia and Eichhornia float on water. Their short side branch carries a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots, ready to become a new plant.

C1.text: Now the pair students mix up: a thorn and a spine.

C2.text: Both are hard and pointed. Both protect the plant from animals.

C3.text: But a thorn is a modified stem, grown from an axillary bud, like in Bougainvillea. A spine in cactus is a modified leaf.

C4.text: Your turn. A pointed thorn sits right in the axil of a leaf, exactly where a bud should be. Stem or leaf? Pause and decide.

C5.text: A stem! It grew from the axillary bud. That is why a Bougainvillea thorn sits in the axil of a leaf.

T1.text: Remember this. Nodes and buds make a stem a stem, even when it hides under the soil.

W1.text: Now, a worked example. Let's name four stems in disguise.

W2.text: Ginger, a thick knob under the soil, full of stored food. That is an underground stem.

W3.text: A grapevine's coiled spring, wrapped around a wire. That is a stem tendril.

W4.text: A sharp, woody point in the axil of a Bougainvillea leaf. That is a stem thorn.

W5.text: The flat green pad of Opuntia, making food in the desert. That is a flattened green stem.

X2.text: Many students think every part that grows under the soil is a root.

X3.text: But potato, ginger and Colocasia grow under the soil, and they are stems. They store food, and they still carry nodes and buds.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As matching a plant with its stem modification, or asking which part a structure came from.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Read the assertion and the reason. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion.

A2.text: Storing food does not make a part a stem. A carrot stores food too, and it is a root.

A3.text: A potato is a stem because its eyes are nodes, with buds that sprout into new shoots.
